rows.name: Abacus
rows.summary: Manual bead reckoner — Rows of beads on rods are slid by hand to add, subtract, multiply, and divide. Each column stands for a place value, so the beads remember the running total.

rows.name: Signature Bead Engine
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Abacus

rows.name: Antikythera Mechanism
rows.summary: Geared astronomical calculator — A box of bronze gears that predicted the positions of the sun and moon, the dates of eclipses, and the cycles of the ancient games. Turning one crank moved pointers across dials on both faces.

rows.name: Signature Sky Dial
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Antikythera Mechanism

rows.name: Pascaline
rows.summary: Mechanical adding machine — A brass box where numbered wheels are turned with a stylus to add and subtract. Carry from one wheel to the next happens automatically inside the gearing.

rows.name: Signature Carry Wheel
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Pascaline

rows.name: Leibniz Stepped Reckoner
rows.summary: Multiplication by stepped drum — Cylindrical drums with teeth of increasing length turn number wheels to multiply and divide, not just add. The operator sets the number on sliders and cranks through the calculation.

rows.name: Signature Stepped Drum
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Leibniz Stepped Reckoner

rows.name: Difference Engine
rows.summary: Polynomial table computer — A gear machine designed to compute mathematical tables by the method of finite differences, stamping results ready for printing. It used only addition and carriage, never multiplication.

rows.name: Signature Difference Engine
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Difference Engine

rows.name: Analytical Engine
rows.summary: Programmable mechanical computer — A design with a mill for arithmetic, a store for memory, and punched cards to direct the sequence of operations — the same three parts a modern computer has. Programs could branch and loop.

rows.name: Signature Mill & Store
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Analytical Engine

rows.name: Jacquard Loom
rows.summary: Punched-card pattern control — A weaving loom whose pattern is set by a chain of punched cards, one card per row of the fabric. Each card's holes decide which threads lift, weaving complex images automatically.

rows.name: Signature Pattern Loom
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Jacquard Loom

rows.name: Hollerith Tabulating Machine
rows.summary: Punched-card census counter — Cards punched with people's data are read electrically by pins dipping through the holes into mercury cups. Dials count each category as cards feed through by hand and later by machine.

rows.name: Signature Card Counter
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Hollerith Tabulating Machine

rows.name: Zuse Z3
rows.summary: Electromechanical program computer — A machine of telephone relays that read programs from punched film. It worked in binary floating point and could run stored instruction sequences automatically.

rows.name: Signature Relay Brain
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Zuse Z3

rows.name: Harvard Mark I
rows.summary: Electromechanical giant — A 51-foot machine of switches, relays, and shafts that computed ballistics and physics tables automatically. It could multiply in about six seconds and printed its answers on punch cards or type.

rows.name: Signature Shaft Computer
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Harvard Mark I

rows.name: Colossus
rows.summary: Electronic code-breaking machine — Two thousand vacuum tubes processed punched tape at high speed to find the settings of an enemy cipher machine. It compared patterns statistically and printed its scores for analysts.

rows.name: Signature Pattern Breaker
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Colossus

rows.name: ENIAC
rows.summary: First general-purpose electronic computer — Seventeen thousand vacuum tubes performed additions at electronic speed, programmed by plugging cables into panels like a telephone switchboard. A calculation that took days by hand finished in seconds.

rows.name: Signature Tube Array
rows.summary: Signature-made version of ENIAC

rows.name: Manchester Baby
rows.summary: First stored-program run — A small machine that held both its instructions and its data in the same electronic memory — the stored-program idea. Its first program, in June 1948, found the highest factor of a number.

rows.name: Signature First Program
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Manchester Baby

rows.name: EDSAC
rows.summary: First practical stored-program service — A mercury-delay-line memory machine that ran real scientific jobs for university researchers, including programs for biology and radio astronomy. Users prepared programs on punched tape.

rows.name: Signature Delay Line
rows.summary: Signature-made version of EDSAC

rows.name: UNIVAC I
rows.summary: First commercial US computer — The first computer sold as a commercial product in the United States, famous for predicting a presidential election result on television. It read metal magnetic tape and printed its output.

rows.name: Signature Census Box
rows.summary: Signature-made version of UNIVAC I

rows.name: IBM 701
rows.summary: IBM's first scientific computer — IBM's first commercial scientific computer, renting to aircraft companies and government labs. It used electrostatic storage tubes for memory and magnetic tape for data.

rows.name: Signature Scientific 52
rows.summary: Signature-made version of IBM 701

rows.name: IBM 650
rows.summary: The workhorse of the 1950s — A drum-memory machine that became the most popular computer of its decade, used for payroll, grades, and science alike. Programs were loaded from punched cards.

rows.name: Signature Drum 650
rows.summary: Signature-made version of IBM 650

rows.name: TX-0
rows.summary: Transistorized research machine — One of the first computers built with transistors instead of vacuum tubes, which made it far smaller and cooler. It gave hackers a machine they could use directly, one at a time.

rows.name: Signature Cool Box
rows.summary: Signature-made version of TX-0

rows.name: PDP-1
rows.summary: Interactive hacker machine — A compact machine with a round cathode-ray display and a light pen, sold to labs that wanted hands-on computing. Programmers wrote the first video game, Spacewar!, on it.

rows.name: Signature Round Screen
rows.summary: Signature-made version of PDP-1

rows.name: IBM System/360
rows.summary: One family, many sizes — A line of compatible computers from small business machines to giant mainframes, all running the same programs. It introduced the 8-bit byte as the industry standard.

rows.name: Signature Family 36
rows.summary: Signature-made version of IBM System/360

rows.name: PDP-8
rows.summary: First true minicomputer — A machine the size of a small refrigerator that a single department could afford and keep. It sold by the tens of thousands and carried computing into labs and factories.

rows.name: Signature Mini 8
rows.summary: Signature-made version of PDP-8

rows.name: Intel 4004
rows.summary: First commercial microprocessor — The whole central processor of a computer on one chip — four bits wide, running at under a megahertz. It was made for a calculator and ended up starting the microprocessor age.

rows.name: Signature Four-Bit
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Intel 4004

rows.name: Intel 8008
rows.summary: Eight-bit step up — An 8-bit processor on one chip that could address far more memory than the 4004. It powered early hobby machines and terminals.

rows.name: Signature Eight-Bit
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Intel 8008

rows.name: Altair 8800
rows.summary: The machine that started home computing — A kit computer with toggle switches on the front and no keyboard or screen at first. Hobbyists flipped in programs bit by bit and watched the lights answer.

rows.name: Signature Toggle Box
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Altair 8800

rows.name: Apple I
rows.summary: Hand-built garage board — A bare circuit board sold without case, keyboard, or power supply — the buyer finished the computer. It displayed text on an ordinary television.

rows.name: Signature Garage Board
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Apple I

rows.name: TRS-80 Model I
rows.summary: The people's computer — A complete home computer sold through Radio Shack stores with keyboard, screen, and cassette storage. Ordinary families could buy one off the shelf.

rows.name: Signature Shack Box
rows.summary: Signature-made version of TRS-80 Model I

rows.name: Apple II
rows.summary: Color computer for everyone — A home computer with color graphics, sound, and slots for expansion cards. It ran the first spreadsheet program, which gave businesses a reason to buy it.

rows.name: Signature Rainbow Slots
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Apple II

rows.name: Osborne 1
rows.summary: First portable computer — A sewing-machine-sized computer with a tiny 5-inch screen and a handle, sold with a bundle of business software. It was luggable before laptops existed.

rows.name: Signature Luggable
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Osborne 1

rows.name: BBC Micro
rows.summary: Britain's classroom computer — A sturdy school computer made for the BBC's computer literacy project, with excellent BASIC and ports for experiments. A generation learned to program on it.

rows.name: Signature School Box
rows.summary: Signature-made version of BBC Micro

rows.name: IBM PC 5150
rows.summary: The template for all PCs — A business machine with an open design that other companies could copy, which created the clone industry. Its slot architecture and DOS software became the world standard.

rows.name: Signature Open 5150
rows.summary: Signature-made version of IBM PC 5150

rows.name: ZX Spectrum
rows.summary: The bedroom coder's machine — A tiny rubber-keyed computer that plugged into the TV and loaded games from cassette tape in minutes. Millions of kids learned to code on it.

rows.name: Signature Rubber Keys
rows.summary: Signature-made version of ZX Spectrum

rows.name: Commodore 64
rows.summary: Best-selling computer ever — Sixty-four kilobytes of memory, famous sound and sprite graphics, and a huge game library. It became the best-selling single computer model of all time.

rows.name: Signature SID Box
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Commodore 64

rows.name: Macintosh 128K
rows.summary: The mouse goes mainstream — The first affordable computer with a graphical screen, windows, and a mouse for ordinary buyers. What you saw on screen was what printed.

rows.name: Signature Friendly Face
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Macintosh 128K

rows.name: Atari ST
rows.summary: Musician's sixteen-bit — A sixteen-bit machine with a crisp monochrome display option and built-in MIDI ports that made it the studio standard for musicians. It brought real power to a home price.

rows.name: Signature Studio ST
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Atari ST

rows.name: Amiga 1000
rows.summary: Multimedia before multimedia — A machine with custom chips for graphics and sound that could do animation and stereo music years ahead of rivals. Video producers used it for titling and effects.

rows.name: Signature Custom Chips
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Amiga 1000

rows.name: Motorola 68000
rows.summary: The 32-bit bridge chip — A processor with a clean 32-bit design inside that powered the Macintosh, the Amiga, the Atari ST, and early workstations. Programmers loved its tidy instruction set.

rows.name: Signature Clean Thirty-Two
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Motorola 68000

rows.name: x86-64 Desktop PC
rows.summary: Everyday powerhouse — The standard home and office computer: a 64-bit processor, gigabytes of memory, and slots for graphics and storage. It runs everything from games to engineering software.

rows.name: Signature Open Tower
rows.summary: Signature-made version of x86-64 Desktop PC

rows.name: ARM Smartphone SoC
rows.summary: A computer in your pocket — A single chip holding the processor, graphics, radio, and memory controller for a phone. It sips power so the battery lasts all day while running demanding apps.

rows.name: Signature Pocket Chip
rows.summary: Signature-made version of ARM Smartphone SoC

rows.name: Apple Silicon Mac
rows.summary: One chip, whole Mac — A Mac where the processor, graphics, and memory live on one efficient chip. It runs cool and quiet while beating older multi-chip designs.

rows.name: Signature Unified One
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Apple Silicon Mac

rows.name: RISC-V Developer Board
rows.summary: Open instruction computer — A computer built on the free and open RISC-V instruction set, so anyone can study and build on its design. It runs Linux and standard software.

rows.name: Signature Open Core
rows.summary: Signature-made version of RISC-V Developer Board

rows.name: GPU Compute Node
rows.summary: Thousands of cores, one job — A server packed with graphics processors that do thousands of simple calculations at once. It trains AI models and renders films in hours instead of months.

rows.name: Signature Thousand Core
rows.summary: Signature-made version of GPU Compute Node

rows.name: Single-Board Computer
rows.summary: Credit-card computer — A complete computer on one small board with ports for screen, USB, and electronics projects. It runs a full operating system from a memory card.

rows.name: Signature Card Computer
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Single-Board Computer

rows.name: Microcontroller Board
rows.summary: One chip, one job — A tiny chip with processor, memory, and input-output pins that runs a single program forever — inside toys, thermostats, and robots. It costs little and sips power.

rows.name: Signature Pin Brain
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Microcontroller Board

rows.name: Game Console SoC
rows.summary: Living-room supercomputer — A custom chip combining a strong processor and graphics to run detailed games on the television. It is tuned for one job: fast, beautiful play.

rows.name: Signature Play Chip
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Game Console SoC

rows.name: Datacenter Server Blade
rows.summary: Rack-scale workhorse — A slim computer that slides into a rack with dozens of siblings, serving websites and files around the clock. It is built for reliability, not looks.

rows.name: Signature Blade Rack
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Datacenter Server Blade

rows.name: AI Accelerator Pod
rows.summary: Number-crunching specialist — A chip designed for one thing: the matrix math that AI runs on. It does in seconds what would take a regular processor hours.

rows.name: Signature Matrix Engine
rows.summary: Signature-made version of AI Accelerator Pod

rows.name: FPGA Development Board
rows.summary: Rewirable hardware — A chip whose logic can be rewired after manufacturing, so it becomes any digital circuit the designer describes. It sits between software and custom chips.

rows.name: Signature Rewire Board
rows.summary: Signature-made version of FPGA Development Board

rows.name: Supercomputer Cluster Node
rows.summary: Teamwork at scale — Thousands of computers linked by fast networks act as one machine for weather, physics, and AI. Each node is ordinary; the teamwork is extraordinary.

rows.name: Signature Team Rack
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Supercomputer Cluster Node

rows.name: Edge AI Device
rows.summary: Smart without the cloud — A small device that runs AI right where it sits — a camera that counts cars, a speaker that hears commands — with no internet needed. Private and instant.

rows.name: Signature Local Mind
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Edge AI Device

rows.name: Automotive Control Unit
rows.summary: The car's hidden computers — Dozens of small rugged computers inside a car manage the engine, brakes, and airbags. They must never crash, so they are built to extreme reliability standards.

rows.name: Signature Road Brain
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Automotive Control Unit

rows.name: Satellite Flight Computer
rows.summary: Computer in orbit — A radiation-hardened computer that flies the spacecraft, aims the antennas, and runs the science instruments. It must work for years with no repair shop.

rows.name: Signature Orbit Box
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Satellite Flight Computer

rows.name: Network Appliance
rows.summary: Traffic cop of the internet — A specialized computer that forwards data packets between networks at wire speed. It is the reason your messages find their way.

rows.name: Signature Packet Post
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Network Appliance

rows.name: Home Storage Server
rows.summary: Your own private cloud — A box of hard drives on the home network that keeps every photo and file safe with automatic copies. It replaces renting cloud storage.

rows.name: Signature Family Vault
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Home Storage Server

rows.name: Laptop SoC System
rows.summary: Desk power, to go — A full computer folded into a portable shape: efficient processor, battery, screen, and keyboard in one. It is the most common personal computer form today.

rows.name: Signature Carry All
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Laptop SoC System

rows.name: Smartwatch Computer
rows.summary: Wrist-sized assistant — A complete computer on the wrist that tracks health, shows messages, and runs apps on a tiny efficient chip. It charges rarely and works all day.

rows.name: Signature Wrist Mind
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Smartwatch Computer

rows.name: E-Reader Board
rows.summary: A library in your hand — A low-power computer built around a paper-like display that holds thousands of books. It reads for weeks on one charge.

rows.name: Signature Paper Library
rows.summary: Signature-made version of E-Reader Board

rows.name: Superconducting Qubit Processor
rows.summary: Frozen lightning logic — Qubits made of superconducting circuits chilled near absolute zero, controlled by microwave pulses. They run quantum algorithms that no regular computer can simulate at scale.

rows.name: Signature Frost Qubit
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Superconducting Qubit Processor

rows.name: Trapped-Ion Processor
rows.summary: Atoms held by lightning — Individual charged atoms float in electromagnetic traps, and lasers flip their quantum states. Ions of the same kind are perfectly identical, which makes them excellent qubits.

rows.name: Signature Ion Cage
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Trapped-Ion Processor

rows.name: Photonic Quantum Processor
rows.summary: Computing with light — Qubits carried by single particles of light race through chips of waveguides and detectors. Photons barely interact with noise, and the chips can work closer to room temperature.

rows.name: Signature Light Loom
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Photonic Quantum Processor

rows.name: Quantum Annealer
rows.summary: Settling into answers — A machine that solves optimization puzzles by letting quantum bits naturally settle into their lowest-energy arrangement. It is built for one kind of math, done extremely well.

rows.name: Signature Settle Solver
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Quantum Annealer

rows.name: Neutral-Atom Array
rows.summary: Tweezers of light — Hundreds of neutral atoms are held in place by focused laser beams like tweezers, then excited to giant Rydberg states to interact. The array can rearrange itself for each problem.

rows.name: Signature Atom Tweezer
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Neutral-Atom Array

rows.name: Silicon Spin Qubit
rows.summary: Quantum dots in silicon — Single electrons trapped in tiny silicon dots use their spin as a qubit. Because they are made with chip-factory methods, they could one day sit beside regular transistors.

rows.name: Signature Dot Spin
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Silicon Spin Qubit

rows.name: NMR Quantum Computer
rows.summary: Molecules as processors — The first machines to run real quantum algorithms used the atomic nuclei inside liquid molecules, read by the same physics as hospital MRI scanners. A famous factoring demo ran on seven qubits.

rows.name: Signature Molecule Lab
rows.summary: Signature-made version of NMR Quantum Computer

rows.name: Diamond NV Quantum Register
rows.summary: Qubits in a gemstone — Atomic-scale defects in diamond hold quantum states that survive at room temperature. They sense magnetic fields with exquisite precision as well as compute.

rows.name: Signature Gem Qubit
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Diamond NV Quantum Register

rows.name: Cold-Atom Quantum Simulator
rows.summary: A universe in a vacuum — Clouds of atoms chilled to near absolute zero mimic the quantum behavior of materials and molecules. Instead of calculating nature, the machine becomes a small piece of it.

rows.name: Signature Chill Chamber
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Cold-Atom Quantum Simulator

rows.name: Rydberg Atom Processor
rows.summary: Giant atoms, strong talk — Atoms puffed up to huge Rydberg states interact powerfully over long distances, making fast quantum gates. Laser tweezers place each atom exactly where the problem needs it.

rows.name: Signature Giant Atom
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Rydberg Atom Processor

rows.name: Hybrid QPU-CPU Appliance
rows.summary: Quantum with a classical co-pilot — A box that pairs a small quantum processor with a regular computer, splitting each job: the classical side prepares and the quantum side solves the hard kernel. They iterate together.

rows.name: Signature Duet Box
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Hybrid QPU-CPU Appliance

rows.name: Topological Qubit Research
rows.summary: Knots that remember — An experimental approach where quantum information is stored in the braided paths of exotic particles, protected from noise by topology itself. It is still laboratory research.

rows.name: Signature Braid Lab
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Topological Qubit Research

rows.name: Silicon CMOS Substrate
rows.summary: The sand that thinks — Purified sand becomes the crystal wafer on which billions of transistors are printed. Complementary pairs of transistors switch with almost no wasted power.

rows.name: Signature Sand Crystal
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Silicon CMOS Substrate

rows.name: Germanium Transistor
rows.summary: The first transistor's home — The very first transistors were built on germanium, which switches at lower voltage than silicon. It ruled the early years before silicon took over.

rows.name: Signature First Crystal
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Germanium Transistor

rows.name: Gallium Arsenide Chip
rows.summary: Speed from exotic crystal — A compound semiconductor that moves electrons far faster than silicon, used in phone radios, lasers, and satellites. It costs more but wins where speed matters.

rows.name: Signature Swift Crystal
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Gallium Arsenide Chip

rows.name: Graphene Transistor
rows.summary: One atom thin — A sheet of carbon one atom thick that conducts electricity better than copper and is stronger than steel. Transistors built on it could switch at extreme speeds.

rows.name: Signature Atom Sheet
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Graphene Transistor

rows.name: Diamond NV-Center Substrate
rows.summary: Quantum gemstone chip — Diamond crystals with single-atom defects hold quantum states at room temperature. They sense magnetic fields atom by atom and can serve as qubits.

rows.name: Signature Gem Wafer
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Diamond NV-Center Substrate

rows.name: Memristor Crossbar Array
rows.summary: Memory that computes — A grid of resistors that remember their resistance, so the memory itself can do the math. Multiplying matrices happens in the wires, not in a processor.

rows.name: Signature Memory Grid
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Memristor Crossbar Array

rows.name: Silicon Photonic Chip
rows.summary: Computing with light on silicon — Light guides etched into silicon carry data as photons instead of electrons, moving information faster with less heat. It already links datacenters; logic is next.

rows.name: Signature Light Roads
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Silicon Photonic Chip

rows.name: DNA Storage-Compute
rows.summary: Data in life's code — Digital files encoded into synthetic DNA strands store staggering amounts of data in a speck of material. Chemical reactions can also run simple computations on the strands.

rows.name: Signature Life Disk
rows.summary: Signature-made version of DNA Storage-Compute

rows.name: Spintronic MRAM Device
rows.summary: Memory from electron spin — Memory cells that store bits in the magnetic direction of electron spins, keeping data with no power. It is fast like RAM and permanent like a disk.

rows.name: Signature Spin Memory
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Spintronic MRAM Device

rows.name: Carbon Nanotube Transistor
rows.summary: Rolled-up wire switches — Transistors made from rolled sheets of carbon atoms, thinner and potentially faster than silicon channels. Whole tiny computers have been built from them in labs.

rows.name: Signature Tube Switch
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Carbon Nanotube Transistor

rows.name: Silicon Carbide Power Device
rows.summary: Tough crystal for power — A hard crystal that switches high voltages and shrugs off heat that would kill silicon. It drives electric cars and solar inverters efficiently.

rows.name: Signature Tough Switch
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Silicon Carbide Power Device

rows.name: Gallium Nitride Device
rows.summary: Tiny chargers, big power — A crystal that switches power at extreme speed, shrinking phone chargers to pocket size. It also makes the blue and white LEDs that light the world.

rows.name: Signature Pocket Power
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Gallium Nitride Device

rows.name: 2D TMD Transistor (MoS2)
rows.summary: Single-layer switches — Transistors built from a single layer of molybdenum disulfide, a crystal that is a natural semiconductor unlike graphene. Stacked layers could build 3D chips.

rows.name: Signature Layer Cake
rows.summary: Signature-made version of 2D TMD Transistor (MoS2)

rows.name: Phase-Change Memory Compute
rows.summary: Glass that remembers — A material that flips between glassy and crystalline states to store bits, and can do arithmetic in the flip itself. It bridges memory and processor.

rows.name: Signature Glass Brain
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Phase-Change Memory Compute

rows.name: Ferroelectric FET
rows.summary: Polarized transistor — A transistor whose gate remembers its electric polarization, storing a bit without power and switching at low voltage. It could make memory as fast as logic.

rows.name: Signature Polar Switch
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Ferroelectric FET

rows.name: Superconducting Logic (RSFQ)
rows.summary: Pulses at light speed — Logic built from superconducting loops that pass single quantum pulses of magnetic flux, switching hundreds of times faster than silicon while barely warming.

rows.name: Signature Flux Pulse
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Superconducting Logic (RSFQ)

rows.name: Plasmonic Waveguide Chip
rows.summary: Light squeezed into metal — Light waves squeezed along metal surfaces carry signals in spaces far smaller than a wavelength. It promises optics at electronic sizes.

rows.name: Signature Squeeze Light
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Plasmonic Waveguide Chip

rows.name: Semiconductor Superlattice
rows.summary: Crystal lasagna — Alternating atomic layers of different semiconductors create artificial crystals with engineered electronic properties. They make precise lasers and detectors.

rows.name: Signature Layer Lasagna
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Semiconductor Superlattice

rows.name: Hybrid Classical-Quantum System
rows.summary: Best of both worlds — A regular computer and a quantum processor work as one team on each problem. The classical side handles data and control; the quantum side attacks the hard core.

rows.name: Signature Duet Engine
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Hybrid Classical-Quantum System

rows.name: Neuromorphic-Digital Hybrid
rows.summary: Brain-like plus exact — A chip of artificial neurons that sips power sits beside a regular processor that handles exact math. Senses go to the neurons; spreadsheets go to the CPU.

rows.name: Signature Brain Plus
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Neuromorphic-Digital Hybrid

rows.name: Analog-Digital Hybrid Computer
rows.summary: Wires that solve equations — Analog circuits integrate and differentiate continuously while a digital side sets up the problem and reads the answer. Old hybrids simulated aircraft and rockets this way.

rows.name: Signature Smooth Plus Exact
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Analog-Digital Hybrid Computer

rows.name: FPGA-CPU Hybrid
rows.summary: Processor with a rewirable twin — A regular processor shares its board with a rewirable logic chip that becomes custom hardware for the hot loop. Software speed where it counts, hardware speed where it matters.

rows.name: Signature Twin Board
rows.summary: Signature-made version of FPGA-CPU Hybrid

rows.name: Co-Packaged Photonic-Electronic
rows.summary: Light and logic, one package — Photonic chips that move data as light sit in the same package as the electronic chips that think. Data flies between them at light speed with little heat.

rows.name: Signature Light Package
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Co-Packaged Photonic-Electronic

rows.name: CPU-GPU Heterogeneous Node
rows.summary: Manager and muscle — A few clever CPU cores direct thousands of simple GPU cores, splitting every job by talent. This pairing powers gaming, AI, and science computing.

rows.name: Signature Manager Muscle
rows.summary: Signature-made version of CPU-GPU Heterogeneous Node

rows.name: Chiplet Multi-Die Package
rows.summary: LEGO-block processors — Instead of one giant chip, several small specialized chips are bonded together in one package and act as one processor. Each chiplet does what it does best.

rows.name: Signature Block Chip
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Chiplet Multi-Die Package

rows.name: ReRAM In-Memory Accelerator
rows.summary: Math inside the memory — A resistive-memory array performs neural-network math where the weights live, beside a small digital controller. Data barely moves, so power plummets.

rows.name: Signature Weight Grid
rows.summary: Signature-made version of ReRAM In-Memory Accelerator

rows.name: Optical Coprocessor + Digital Host
rows.summary: Light does the heavy math — An optical chip performs matrix math at the speed of light while a regular computer feeds it data and collects answers. Fourier transforms happen literally at light speed.

rows.name: Signature Prism Math
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Optical Coprocessor + Digital Host

rows.name: Wafer-Scale Engine + Host
rows.summary: A whole wafer, one computer — An entire silicon wafer is used as a single giant chip, surrounded by memory and a host computer. AI models too big for normal chips fit whole.

rows.name: Signature Whole Wafer
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Wafer-Scale Engine + Host

rows.name: Photonic Exascale Computer
rows.summary: A billion billion light-ops — A future machine that does exascale arithmetic with photons instead of electrons, in chips of waveguides and modulators. SPECULATION: no such complete machine exists.

rows.name: Signature Sun Computer
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Photonic Exascale Computer

rows.name: Room-Temperature Superconductor Logic
rows.summary: Cold-free super logic — Logic gates from a superconductor that works at room temperature would switch at enormous speed with no cooling at all. SPECULATION: no verified room-temperature superconductor exists.

rows.name: Signature Warm Flux
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Room-Temperature Superconductor Logic

rows.name: Large-Scale DNA Computer
rows.summary: Vats that compute — A future computer where vats of DNA strands run massively parallel computations by chemistry, storing exabytes in a thimble. SPECULATION: only tiny demos exist today.

rows.name: Signature Life Vat
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Large-Scale DNA Computer

rows.name: Molecular Electronics Computer
rows.summary: Single-molecule switches — A computer whose switches are individual molecules wired between electrodes, packing logic at the ultimate density. SPECULATION: reliable molecular circuits do not exist yet.

rows.name: Signature Molecule Mesh
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Molecular Electronics Computer

rows.name: Quantum Internet Node
rows.summary: Entanglement on tap — A future network box that shares entanglement between distant cities, enabling unhackable keys and linked quantum computers. SPECULATION: only research links exist.

rows.name: Signature Entangle Post
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Quantum Internet Node

rows.name: Brain-Scale Neuromorphic System
rows.summary: A cortex in a cabinet — A future machine with as many artificial neurons as a human brain, running on brain-like power budgets. SPECULATION: today's biggest systems are far smaller.

rows.name: Signature Cortex Cabinet
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Brain-Scale Neuromorphic System

rows.name: Reversible Adiabatic Computer
rows.summary: Computing without heat — A future computer that never erases information, dodging the fundamental heat limit of logic. It would run cool forever, in principle. SPECULATION: only lab demos exist.

rows.name: Signature Unerase Engine
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Reversible Adiabatic Computer

rows.name: All-Spin Logic Processor
rows.summary: Magnets doing math — A future processor where magnetic spins do the logic with no charge current at all, promising instant-on computers that sip power. SPECULATION: spin logic is still laboratory research.

rows.name: Signature Spin Abacus
rows.summary: Signature-made version of All-Spin Logic Processor

rows.name: Single-Molecule Switch Array
rows.summary: One molecule, one bit — A memory where each bit is a single switchable molecule, reaching densities no lithography can touch. SPECULATION: stable arrays do not exist yet.

rows.name: Signature Molecule Page
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Single-Molecule Switch Array

rows.name: Terahertz Transistor Computer
rows.summary: A trillion switches a second — A future machine whose transistors switch at terahertz rates — a thousand times today's gigahertz. SPECULATION: no complete terahertz computer exists.

rows.name: Signature Blink Engine
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Terahertz Transistor Computer

rows.name: Skyrmion Racetrack Memory-Compute
rows.summary: Magnetic whirlpools that work — A future device where tiny magnetic whirlpools race along tracks, storing and processing data as they move. SPECULATION: controlled skyrmion circuits are still research.

rows.name: Signature Whirlpool Track
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Skyrmion Racetrack Memory-Compute

rows.name: Cryogenic CMOS Control Chip
rows.summary: The quantum machine's butler — A future chip that lives in the fridge beside qubits, translating room-temperature commands into the delicate pulses qubits need. Near-term: prototypes exist in labs.

rows.name: Signature Frost Butler
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Cryogenic CMOS Control Chip

rows.name: Signature Lattice Computer
rows.summary: The crystal that computes — His original machine: a three-dimensional lattice of tiny switches where data flows along crystal paths instead of wires. Every layer of the lattice is both memory and processor, so nothing ever travels far.

rows.name: Signature Lattice Computer
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Signature Lattice Computer

rows.name: Signature Qubit Loom
rows.summary: Weaving quantum answers — His original quantum design: qubits are threads on a loom, and quantum gates are the shuttle weaving them into entangled fabric. The pattern of the weave IS the program, readable at a glance.

rows.name: Signature Qubit Loom
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Signature Qubit Loom

rows.name: Signature Paradox Immune Core
rows.summary: Logic that cannot contradict itself — His original processor core: every instruction is checked by a twin circuit before it runs, so paradoxes and contradictions are caught and resolved, never executed. It is the hardware heart of his paradox-immune system.

rows.name: Signature Paradox Immune Core
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Signature Paradox Immune Core

rows.name: Signature Deterministic Cascade
rows.summary: No randomness, ever — His original engine: a cascade of deterministic stages where the same input always gives the same output, down to the last bit. It proves its answers by replaying them, step for step, on demand.

rows.name: Signature Deterministic Cascade
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Signature Deterministic Cascade

rows.name: Signature Hexfold Memory
rows.summary: Memory folded like honeycomb — His original memory: storage cells folded into hexagonal prisms, packing more bits per area than square grids. Each hex cell knows its six neighbors, so data can flow in any direction.

rows.name: Signature Hexfold Memory
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Signature Hexfold Memory

rows.name: Signature Deterministic Fabric
rows.summary: A whole computer of proof — His original system architecture: processor, memory, and interconnect woven into one deterministic fabric where every signal's path is known in advance. Nothing is left to chance, ever.

rows.name: Signature Deterministic Fabric
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Signature Deterministic Fabric

rows.name: Signature Swarm Gate Array
rows.summary: A million tiny deciders — His original array: thousands of tiny simple gates that vote on every decision like a swarm, so no single failure can corrupt an answer. The swarm re-routes around dead gates automatically.

rows.name: Signature Swarm Gate Array
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Signature Swarm Gate Array

rows.name: Signature Cellular Automata Plane
rows.summary: The universe as a grid — His original plane: a vast grid of cells following his own rule-set, growing patterns that compute. Programs are starting patterns; answers are the shapes the grid settles into.

rows.name: Signature Cellular Automata Plane
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Signature Cellular Automata Plane

rows.name: Signature Neural Loom
rows.summary: AI woven, not programmed — His original AI machine: neural networks are woven on a loom-like frame where each thread is a connection with an adjustable weight. Training is literally re-weaving, visible to the eye.

rows.name: Signature Neural Loom
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Signature Neural Loom

rows.name: Signature Hybrid Fusion Core
rows.summary: All eleven lenses, one chip — His original fusion processor: eleven computing lenses — deterministic, probabilistic, geometric, hash, neural, evolutionary, fuzzy, swarm, decision-tree, cellular, and hybrid fusion — on one chip, voting on every answer.

rows.name: Signature Hybrid Fusion Core
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Signature Hybrid Fusion Core

rows.name: Signature Temporal Register Stack
rows.summary: Memory that remembers when — His original registers: a stack where every value carries its own timestamp, so the processor can reach back to any past state without saving snapshots. Time travel for data, built in.

rows.name: Signature Temporal Register Stack
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Signature Temporal Register Stack

rows.name: Signature Probability Collapse Unit
rows.summary: Chance, tamed — His original unit: a probabilistic engine that collapses chance into certainty by running every branch deterministically and keeping the proven winner. Randomness in, proof out.

rows.name: Signature Probability Collapse Unit
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Signature Probability Collapse Unit

rows.name: Signature Golden Ratio ALU
rows.summary: Math in nature's proportion — His original arithmetic unit: an ALU that encodes numbers in golden-ratio base, where multiplication by phi is just a shift. It finds the elegant path through every calculation.

rows.name: Signature Golden Ratio ALU
rows.summary: Signature-made version of Signature Golden Ratio ALU
